strengths.title: Proficient Python programming
strengths.why_it_matters: Python is the core language for building, training, and serving ML models, and strong Python skills let you implement data pipelines and model logic efficiently.
strengths.evidence_quote: Built demand forecasting models in Python.

strengths.title: Hands‑on deep‑learning with PyTorch
strengths.why_it_matters: PyTorch is the primary framework for developing the CNN models the role requires, and your experience scaling to 200k images shows you can handle large‑scale image training.
strengths.evidence_quote: Trained PyTorch CNN models for fruit grading on 200,000 images

strengths.title: Production‑grade model deployment using Docker
strengths.why_it_matters: Deploying models as containerised REST services is a core responsibility; Docker expertise ensures you can ship reliable, reproducible services.
strengths.evidence_quote: Deployed models to production as Docker containers behind a REST service.

strengths.title: Experiment tracking with MLflow
strengths.why_it_matters: MLflow provides reproducibility and version control for experiments, a must‑have for building trustworthy training pipelines.
strengths.evidence_quote: Tracked experiments and model versions with MLflow.

strengths.title: SQL data‑wrangling for training sets
strengths.why_it_matters: Creating high‑quality labelled datasets from metadata stores is essential for image‑based models; solid SQL skills let you extract and clean data reliably.
strengths.evidence_quote: Wrote SQL queries to build labelled training sets from the image metadata database.

questions: Your training loss is not decreasing. How do you systematically debug the issue?
What techniques do you use to prevent overfitting when training a CNN on 200,000 images?
A deployment broke production. What steps do you take to diagnose and restore service?
Explain how you would containerise a PyTorch model and expose it via a REST API.
How do you use MLflow to keep experiments reproducible and shareable across a team?
Describe a situation where you had to roll back to a previous model version in production.

likely_questions.topic: Nice‑to‑have skill gap – Kubernetes & distributed training
questions: The team is considering moving model serving to a Kubernetes cluster. What factors would you evaluate before adopting it?
If you needed to train a model across multiple GPUs or nodes, how would you set up distributed training in PyTorch?
Tell me about a time you had to balance speed of delivery with model quality. How did you decide what to prioritize?
Give an example of how you handled ambiguous requirements when building a data pipeline for training.

prep_plan.focus: Kubernetes basics and when to use it
tasks: Read the Kubernetes overview on the official docs (use any free intro you have).
Map your current Docker deployment workflow to a simple k8s manifest (Deployment + Service).
Identify three pros and three cons of moving your model serving to Kubernetes.
Study the “Distributed Training” chapter in Dive into Deep Learning (D2L).
Create a minimal PyTorch script that uses DistributedDataParallel on two GPUs (can be simulated locally).
Write a short note on how you would monitor training across nodes.
Complete the first two lessons of the Hugging Face LLM Course to grasp transformer basics.
Sketch how you could adapt your image‑grading pipeline to an NLP classification task.
Prepare a one‑minute explanation of the difference between fine‑tuning and RAG.
Review Docker Get Started guide and add a multi‑stage build to your existing Dockerfile.
Practice explaining the end‑to‑end flow: from PyTorch model to Docker container to REST service.
Write a concise bullet‑point summary of your production deployment metrics and monitoring.
Add a custom MLflow tag for dataset version to one of your past experiments.
Create a one‑page cheat sheet of MLflow commands you use most often.
Re‑run a previous experiment from scratch using only the MLflow run ID.
Do a 30‑minute timed mock interview covering the five question topics above.
Record yourself and note any hesitations or gaps in detail.
Refine your STAR stories for the behavioral questions using the MIT STAR guide.
Review feedback from the mock interview and adjust answers where needed.
Finalize a one‑page cheat sheet covering Kubernetes pros/cons, distributed training steps, and key MLflow commands.
Get a good night’s rest and visualize a confident interview performance.
